newsitem.title: ANTIGUA AND BARBUDA: Caricom sets new EU negotiating strategy.
newsitem.headline: Caricom sets new EU negotiating strategy.

text.p: Leaders of the 14-member Caribbean Community (Caricom), along with the presidents of Haiti and the Dominican Republic, forged a common front to negotiate a new Lome trade-and-aid accord with the European Union, officials said on Friday.

The region is unanimous in opposing any proposals from the European Union to break up the 70-member African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) group of Lome beneficiaries into three separate region-specific accords.
With suggestions that South Africa be included in any subsequent Lome agreements, the Caribbean fears the bulk of the available aid would go to Africa.

"If the Europeans did that, Africa would be like the elephant in Lome, with the Caribbean and the Pacific the ears of the elephant," said one senior Caribbean official, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Caricom agreed to send a delegation led by at least one prime minister to the next Organization of African Unity summit in Harare in June to present the Caribbean's proposal that the ACP be retained as a single entity.

Jamaica's prime minister P.J. Patterson said the Caribbean also agreed to lobby for an extension of the next Lome accord beyond the current 10-year period so that relations with the European Union can take place "on a more stable and predictable basis."
A number of trade arrangements with the EU have come under threat recently.
The United States has challenged the region's special banana export regime to Europe before the World Trade Organisation.

And Washington dealt the Caribbean another blow, when it got the WTO to agree to include rum in any agreement on eliminating tariffs on distilled spirits. Regional rum producers enjoy special preferences in Europe, but the new WTO decision would phase out preferences ahead of the timetable agreed with the EU.
The Lome IV accord is set to expire in 2000.
Patterson said Caricom must "prepare the strongest common negotiating position possible" to win retention of the trade arrangements, and even expand them to include services.

The EU banana regime in particular is critical to the four Windward Island states of the eastern Caribbean, accounting for half to two-thirds of total export earnings. Jamaica and Barbados have been the major beneficiaries under the rum protocol.

Caricom invited Preval and Fernandez to attend the next Caricom summit in July in Jamaica for further discussions on a common Lome position. EU commissioner for development Joao Pinhiero was also invited to the July meeting.
